bug_semantics: On a fresh instance with no password configured, check_auth() deliberately admitted every request. POST /api/settings nevertheless accepted the ownership-establishing _set_password pseudo-setting: save_settings() hashed the attacker-chosen value into settings.json as password_hash, turning authentication on. A remote unauthenticated first caller could therefore choose the initial credential, authenticate (and, after the later session-continuity change, receive a session immediately), and lock out the intended operator. The missing invariant was that the unauthenticated disabled-auth state must not permit a non-local client to perform the transition that establishes the first trust root.
flaw_origin: The optional-password feature commit introduced both halves of the flaw together: api/auth.py made check_auth() return true whenever no password existed, while api/config.py made the already-generic /api/settings save path interpret untrusted _set_password as authority to persist the first password. It added no locality, bootstrap token, or existing-owner check around that transition. A later commit only added automatic cookie issuance; it did not originate the takeover because an attacker could already log in with the password they selected.
ai_marker: BIC commit object trailer: "Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.6 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>". The same object identifies human author and committer Nathan Esquenazi <nesquena@gmail.com>; no inference from PR prose, branch names, or later commits is used.
evidence: The first-party advisory GHSA-p52p-4vmg-4vq3 (also CVE-2026-49973) identifies versions before v0.51.358, PRs https://github.com/nesquena/hermes-webui/pull/3964 and https://github.com/nesquena/hermes-webui/pull/3973, advisory fix merge https://github.com/nesquena/hermes-webui/commit/1126e541325d401538f6a272a9c024c37d47ae08, and release https://github.com/nesquena/hermes-webui/releases/tag/v0.51.358. PR #3964 documents the attack path: disabled auth admits POST /api/settings, _set_password persists the first password, and the requester can obtain a session and ownership.

Commit-object and patch inspection of b8b62722ec2f6b3cd394737ab409c35650f29ca6 ("feat: Sprint 19 — password auth, security headers, login page") shows the causal additions: api/auth.py added check_auth() with `if not is_auth_enabled(): return True`; api/config.py added password_hash and save_settings() handling that pops _set_password and writes its hash; static/ui.js posted the password to /api/settings; and server.py placed check_auth() before POST routing. This is the smallest public commit that first made the generic settings request establish the initial credential.

Immediate-parent tree verification at 1c6db07c2bef8d53656032a2c39a2385a176c959 found no _set_password, password_hash, check_auth, or HERMES_WEBUI_PASSWORD in api/config.py, api/routes.py, or server.py. The parent api/routes.py did already contain POST /api/settings at lines 307-309 as `return j(handler, save_settings(body))`, but unknown _set_password had no effect. The BIC diff adds the special interpretation and disabled-auth admission; therefore the vulnerable mechanism is absent in the direct parent, not merely moved or renamed.

History cross-check distinguishes the later b8b-like-looking continuity work: 8b857d9efc121586f2ef79ca4b8f92d8ad373b5b (2026-04-14, "login-module-patch: sync to v0.50.36-local.1") added immediate session-cookie issuance after first password setup, but its parent already accepted and persisted _set_password. It amplified convenience for the requester but was not required for takeover, because the requester could authenticate normally using the chosen password. Thus it is not the BIC.

Tag ancestry verifies the introduction boundary exactly: v0.20 resolves to 1c6db07c2bef8d53656032a2c39a2385a176c959, the BIC's immediate parent; merge-base(BIC, v0.20) is that parent. v0.21 resolves to 51bcf8fead50e120fb26d9f7ecf591e6482baf15 and merge-base(BIC, v0.21) is the BIC itself. `git for-each-ref --contains=<BIC> --sort=version:refname` starts at v0.21, so the flaw enters released history there and remains within the advisory's pre-v0.51.358 affected range.

Fix inspection shows direct content commit f2ef2851d389cf7a41308dcf0180d7cfbe446379 has parent 5dceb2993cc0a6bc42697a30d370425db482609a, exactly tag v0.51.357. In api/routes.py it snapshots auth_enabled_before and, before save_settings(), rejects `requested_password and not auth_enabled_before` unless _onboarding_gate_allows() accepts a local/private client or explicit HERMES_WEBUI_ONBOARDING_OPEN opt-in. Its tree f38bf7aca081dfa3ecaf78c90968a5915ebcb83c equals the tree of advisory merge 1126e541325d401538f6a272a9c024c37d47ae08, exactly tag v0.51.358. Ancestry checks confirm the BIC is in v0.51.357 and the direct fix is in v0.51.358.

`git cat-file -p b8b62722ec2f6b3cd394737ab409c35650f29ca6` gives one parent, author/committer Nathan Esquenazi, and the exact AI co-author trailer `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.6 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>`. The commit directly writes the flawed mechanism, so the AI decision is based solely on BIC commit-object evidence.
reasoning: Vulnerability-first reconstruction begins at the ownership transition, not at the later cookie behavior. Before authentication is configured, the middleware intentionally permits all clients. The flaw occurs when that unauthenticated state is combined with the generic settings endpoint's newly added _set_password interpretation: a remote request can create the very credential that subsequent middleware treats as proof of ownership. History of api/config.py and api/routes.py places the first such combination in b8b62722ec2f6b3cd394737ab409c35650f29ca6. Its direct parent has the generic settings route but none of the auth/password pseudo-setting machinery, directly proving parent absence. Later password hardening and the 8b857d9 session-continuity patch retain the already-vulnerable bootstrap and therefore are not smaller origins. Release ancestry independently brackets the lifecycle from v0.20 (parent/absent) to v0.21 (BIC present), through vulnerable v0.51.357, and then to direct guard f2ef2851d389cf7a41308dcf0180d7cfbe446379 and advisory merge/tag v0.51.358. Because the BIC itself has an explicit Claude Opus Co-Authored-By trailer and directly introduced both the permissive disabled-auth boundary and the unauthenticated ownership-setting action, the protocol's commit-object-only rule supports AI_ROOT_CAUSE.
